content: Ampicillin Trihydrate is indicated for the treatment of infections caused by susceptible strains of specific organisms. These include: 1. Infections of the genitourinary tract, including gonorrhea: Ampicillin is effective against Escherichia coli (E. coli), Proteus mirabilis (P. mirabilis), enterococci, Shigella, Salmonella typhosa and other Salmonella species, as well as non-penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae (N. gonorrhoeae). 2. Infections of the respiratory tract: It is used to treat infections caused by non-penicillinase-producing Haemophilus influenzae (H. influenzae), staphylococci, and streptococci, including Streptococcus pneumoniae. 3. Infections of the gastrointestinal tract: Ampicillin is effective against Shigella, Salmonella typhosa and other Salmonella species, E. coli, P. mirabilis, and enterococci. 4. Meningitis: It is indicated for infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis (N. meningitidis). To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and to maintain the effectiveness of ampicillin and other antibacterial drugs, ampicillin should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform the empiric choice of therapy. Bacteriological studies should be conducted to identify the causative organisms and determine their susceptibility to ampicillin. Therapy with ampicillin may be initiated before the results of susceptibility testing are available.
